guide.title: Hackney, London: the Museum of the Home, Sutton House, the Hackney Empire and Abney Park Cemetery
guide.intro: Hackney is a London borough running from Shoreditch on the City fringe north to Stoke Newington and east to the River Lea. The National Heritage List records 552 listed-building entries inside the borough boundary, 8 of them Grade I and 30 Grade II*. Sir Robert Geffrye's almshouses of 1714 on Kingsland Road opened as a museum on 2 April 1914 and reopened in June 2021 as the Museum of the Home. Sutton House on Homerton High Street was built in 1535 for Sir Ralph Sadler. Frank Matcham's Hackney Empire opened at 291 Mare Street on 9 December 1901. Abney Park Cemetery opened in 1840 and is registered at Grade II across 12.59 hectares, and Hackney Marshes carries 82 pitches beside the Lea. London Overground's Mildmay, Weaver and Windrush lines cross the borough.

sections.heading: Shoreditch and Hoxton
sections.body:
Kingsland Road, Hoxton Street and Old Street carry the almshouses, churches and civic halls of Hackney's City fringe, and they predate the nightlife.

The Museum of the Home occupies the Geffrye almshouses at 136 Kingsland Road: fourteen four-room houses of 1714 for up to 56 pensioners, built for widows of ironmongers with a large garden behind. The London County Council opened them as a museum on 2 April 1914 to serve the local furniture trade with a reference collection of furniture and interiors. The building closed in January 2018 for an £18 million redevelopment and reopened in June 2021 with 80 per cent more exhibition space and 50 per cent more public space. It opens 10am to 5pm, Tuesday to Sunday and on Bank Holiday Mondays, and the operator states: "Entry is free. No booking is required to visit." The almshouses are Grade I listed, NHLE 1226772; the forecourt wall, gates and railings are Grade II, NHLE 1265688, the niche in the north-west corner of the forecourt Grade II*, NHLE 1265687, and the two K6 telephone kiosks outside Grade II, NHLE 1235680 and 1235681.

St Leonard's Shoreditch stands at the junction of Shoreditch High Street and Hackney Road, a working parish church by George Dance the Elder and one of the eight Grade I entries inside the borough boundary, NHLE 1235382. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here. Shoreditch Town Hall at 380 Old Street, Grade II listed, NHLE 1235232, is let as eight distinct hireable spaces and runs on its programme rather than on general opening hours. Hoxton Hall at 130 Hoxton Street was built in 1863 by James Mortimer in the traditional music hall architectural style, bought by James McDonald in 1866, and enlarged in 1867 with a new upper balcony and the rear balcony extended on both sides; it is Grade II* listed, NHLE 1226830.

Two playhouse sites lie beneath the streets here: The Theatre Playhouse, NHLE 1433271, and The Curtain Playhouse, NHLE 1463328. Both are scheduled monuments, which carry a list entry number and no grade.

sections.heading: Hackney Central and London Fields
sections.body:
Mare Street and the Narrow Way hold the civic and market core, and the ground runs south past London Fields to Broadway Market and the Regent's Canal.

Sutton House at 2 and 4 Homerton High Street was built in 1535 by Sir Ralph Sadler, Principal Secretary of State to Henry VIII, and was first known as Bryck Place. The National Trust bought it in the 1930s with the proceeds of a bequest from William Alexander Robertson, made in memory of his two brothers killed in the First World War. Its linenfold panelling was stolen in the 1980s while the building stood derelict and was returned by the salvage firm that recognised its quality; restoration was completed in 1993 and the house fully opened to the public in 1994. The Linenfold Parlour, the Great Chamber, the Georgian Parlour, a Tudor kitchen and a recreated squatters' room from the 1980s occupation are on show. The house is Grade II* listed, NHLE 1226810, with the gate and piers separately Grade II, NHLE 1226767, and opening comes as a per-date calendar rather than fixed weekly hours.

St Augustine's Tower stands in St John's Church Gardens off Mare Street and opens on the last Sunday of every month except December, 2pm to 4.30pm. It is all that survives above ground of the medieval parish church of St Augustine, Grade I listed, NHLE 1265635. The parish moved in the 1790s to St John-at-Hackney on Lower Clapton Road, James Spiller's church, Grade II* listed, NHLE 1226959, which works as a parish church and as a live-music venue. Five structures in its churchyard carry their own entries on the National Heritage List, among them the war memorial, NHLE 1391701, and the Beaufort, Hunter and Loddiges family tombs, NHLE 1391333, 1391334 and 1391335.

The Hackney Empire at 291 Mare Street opened on 9 December 1901 to a design by Frank Matcham and takes 1268 seated or 1631 standing across Stalls, Dress Circle, Upper Circle and Gallery. ATV converted it to television studios in the mid-1950s, broadcasting Take Your Pick and Oh, Boy!; the Mecca Organisation ran it as a bingo hall from 1963 to 1984; Roland Muldoon's campaign secured the freehold in 1986, and a £17 million refurbishment by Tim Ronalds Architects reopened it in 2004 with an orchestra pit and a studio theatre. The box office opens Monday to Friday, 10am to 6pm, or from two hours before all shows. Broadway Market trades 0900 to 1700 on Saturday and 1000 to 1600 on Sunday, 52 weeks a year, on a street that has held market traders since the 1890s and follows an old drovers' route into the City; F Cooke's eel, pie and mash shop there is Grade II listed, NHLE 1458716.

sections.heading: Dalston and Stoke Newington
sections.body:
Kingsland High Street runs north into Stoke Newington Church Street, and the day divides between a working Art Deco cinema, a Victorian garden cemetery and Clissold Park.

The Rio Cinema at 107 Kingsland High Street is run by a private company limited by guarantee, registered charity number 277415, and the building is Grade II listed, NHLE 1244939. A cinema opened on the site in 1909 as the Kingsland Palace; the present building dates from 1915, when the Kingsland Empire opened, and F. E. Bromige designed the Art Deco remodelling of the frontage and auditorium in 1937. Screen 1 seats 402, 188 in the stalls and 214 in the circle, and a 28-seat Screen 2 opened in the basement in December 2017. The operator publishes a telephone line, 020 7241 9410, open 2pm to 8pm daily.

Abney Park Cemetery at 219 Stoke Newington High Street opened in 1840 and opens daily from 8am to dusk, including Christmas Day and New Year's Day. It is a Grade II registered park and garden, NHLE 1000789, of 12.59 hectares, about 31 acres, laid out as a nondenominational garden cemetery with no dividing lines between religious groups and planted as an arboretum of about 2,500 trees and shrubs, arranged alphabetically and labelled. Roughly 200,000 burials have taken place, 196,843 of them recorded up to the year 2000. William Hosking designed the mortuary chapel with Joseph Bonomi the Younger and George Collison II and it was complete by 1840; the chapel is Grade II listed, NHLE 1265023. Fourteen monuments inside carry their own Grade II entries, among them William and Catherine Booth, NHLE 1257360, and Isaac Watts, NHLE 1235434.

Clissold Park opened as a public park in 1889 and is a Grade II registered park and garden, NHLE 1000800, of 22.74 hectares, with the New River running through it. The council names an aviary and animal enclosures, a paddling area, tennis courts, a wheels park, a pond-dipping platform and an organic growing space among its facilities. Clissold House holds a café and hireable rooms and is Grade II* listed, NHLE 1226509, under the list name Refreshment Rooms; house and park were restored in a project estimated at £8.9 million, begun in 2010 and funded by the Heritage Lottery Fund, the council and the Big Lottery Fund. The park opens by 7.30am year-round and closes between 5pm in January and December and 9.30pm from May to August. On Green Lanes the Castle Climbing Centre occupies the former Metropolitan Water Board engine house, built in the form of a castle for the Stoke Newington reservoirs and Grade II* listed, NHLE 1226755; it opens Monday to Friday 8am to 10pm, weekends 9am to 8pm and bank holidays 8am to 10pm, with a café and a garden.

sections.heading: Clapton and the Lea Valley
sections.body:
East of Lower Clapton Road the streets give out onto marsh, reservoir and towpath along the River Lea.

The Round Chapel at 1D Glenarm Road is the former Clapton Park United Reformed Church, Grade II* listed, NHLE 1265632, and one of the 38 Grade I and Grade II* entries inside the borough boundary. Hackney Historic Buildings Trust runs it as an events and performance venue and hosts music, film and fashion productions there as well as community events. No source states general opening hours, so none are given here.

Hackney Marshes is free, unenclosed common land beside the River Lea with 24-hour access, addressed by Hackney Council at Homerton Road, E9 5PF. The council counts 82 football, rugby and cricket pitches across North Marsh, South Marsh and Mabley Green, describes the marshes as internationally known as the spiritual home of Sunday league football, and the site holds a Green Flag award.

Springfield Park opened as a public park in 1905, formed from the grounds of three private houses of which Springfield House survives, and slopes down to the River Lea and the Springfield Marina. It is a Grade II registered park and garden, NHLE 1000839, of 13.44 hectares, while the council gives the managed park as 14.73 hectares. The park is open at all hours, and Springfield House and its café open 10am to 6pm from April to September and 10am to 4pm from October to March.

Victoria Park adjoins Hackney and is a Tower Hamlets park, a Grade II* registered park and garden, NHLE 1000178, with the Baroness Burdett-Coutts drinking fountain inside it Grade II*, NHLE 1235552.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
London Overground runs three lines across Hackney. Catch the Mildmay line for Dalston Kingsland, Hackney Central, Homerton and Hackney Wick; the Weaver line, shared with Greater Anglia services, for Hackney Downs, London Fields, Rectory Road, Stoke Newington and Clapton; and the Windrush line for Dalston Junction, Haggerston, Hoxton and Shoreditch High Street. Old Street on the Northern line and Liverpool Street, which carries the Central, Circle, Hammersmith & City, Metropolitan and Elizabeth lines, lie beyond the borough's southern boundary, and Manor House on the Piccadilly line serves the Clissold Park side.

For Shoreditch and Hoxton, take the Windrush line to Hoxton, 294 m from the Museum of the Home, or to Shoreditch High Street, 638 m from the centre of the area; Old Street is 823 m, Haggerston 1,084 m and Liverpool Street 1,263 m from the same point.

For Hackney Central and London Fields, Hackney Central is 74 m from the centre of the area, Hackney Downs 448 m, London Fields 678 m and Homerton 875 m. London Fields is 156 m from Broadway Market, and Sutton House stands 431 m from Hackney Central and 540 m from Homerton, both on the Mildmay line.

For Dalston and Stoke Newington, Dalston Junction is 16 m and Dalston Kingsland 244 m from the centre of Dalston, with Canonbury 1,228 m away on the Mildmay and Windrush lines. Stoke Newington on the Weaver line is 329 m from Abney Park Cemetery and Rectory Road 662 m from Stoke Newington's centre; Manor House on the Piccadilly line is 1,254 m from Clissold Park.

For Clapton and the Lea Valley, take the Weaver line to Clapton, 101 m from the centre of the area and the station to use for both the Round Chapel and Springfield Park. Hackney Marshes lies 1,192 m from Homerton on the Mildmay line and 1,201 m from Lea Bridge, which Greater Anglia serves. Hackney Wick, on the Mildmay line, is 78 m from Hackney Wick itself.

faq.question: Is the Museum of the Home free, and when does it open?
faq.answer: Yes. The operator states: "Entry is free. No booking is required to visit." It opens 10am to 5pm, Tuesday to Sunday and on Bank Holiday Mondays, at 136 Kingsland Road, E2 8EA. The buildings are the Geffrye almshouses of 1714, Grade I listed, NHLE 1226772, and the museum reopened in June 2021 after an £18 million redevelopment that added 80 per cent more exhibition space and 50 per cent more public space.

faq.question: When can you go up St Augustine's Tower?
faq.answer: On the last Sunday of every month except December, 2pm to 4.30pm. The tower stands in St John's Church Gardens off Mare Street and is Grade I listed, NHLE 1265635, listed on 24 April 1951 as the Old Tower of Former Church of St Augustine. The custodians' site dates the structure to 1275 and Wikidata records an inception of 1550; no source states which is right, so no construction date is given here.

faq.question: Are Victoria Park and Columbia Road in Hackney?
faq.answer: No. Victoria Park adjoins Hackney but is a Tower Hamlets park, a Grade II* registered park and garden, NHLE 1000178, and the Baroness Burdett-Coutts drinking fountain inside it is Grade II*, NHLE 1235552. Columbia Road and its flower market are a Tower Hamlets street; 2-12 Columbia Road and Leopold Buildings there are Grade II listed, NHLE 1242116.

faq.question: How many listed buildings does Hackney have?
faq.answer: The National Heritage List records 552 listed-building entries inside the Hackney borough boundary: 514 at Grade II, 30 at Grade II* and 8 at Grade I. Three registered parks and gardens fall inside it as well, all at Grade II: Abney Park Cemetery, NHLE 1000789, at 12.59 hectares, Clissold Park, NHLE 1000800, at 22.74 hectares, and Springfield Park, NHLE 1000839, at 13.44 hectares.

faq.question: Which trains reach Hackney Central and Dalston?
faq.answer: London Overground's Mildmay line serves Dalston Kingsland, Hackney Central, Homerton and Hackney Wick. The Windrush line serves Dalston Junction, Haggerston, Hoxton and Shoreditch High Street. The Weaver line, shared with Greater Anglia, serves Hackney Downs, London Fields, Rectory Road, Stoke Newington and Clapton. Dalston Junction stands 16 m and Dalston Kingsland 244 m from the centre of Dalston, and Hackney Central 74 m from the centre of Hackney Central.

faq.question: Which Hackney venues work to a programme rather than opening hours?
faq.answer: St Leonard's Shoreditch, Hoxton Hall, Shoreditch Town Hall, St John-at-Hackney and the Round Chapel all run on a programme of services or events. No source states general opening hours for any of them, so none are given here. Sutton House publishes a per-date calendar rather than fixed weekly hours, and the Rio Cinema publishes a telephone line, 020 7241 9410, open 2pm to 8pm daily.

photos.title: Museum of the Home, 136 Kingsland Road, Hackney
photos.description: The centre of the almshouse range seen head-on from the forecourt, with a pedimented brick centrepiece carrying a clock face, a bell turret above and a statue standing in a niche over the doorway. Long two-storey brick wings with sash windows and ivy along their base run away to either side, and plane trees frame the paved path leading to the entrance.
photos.author: Hjamesberglen

places.name: Museum of the Home
places.summary: The Museum of the Home occupies the former Geffrye almshouses at 136 Kingsland Road and opens 10am to 5pm, Tuesday to Sunday and on Bank Holiday Mondays. The operator states: "Entry is free. No booking is required to visit." The almshouses are Grade I listed, NHLE 1226772, listed on 3 January 1950 under the name The Geffrye Museum. The forecourt wall, gates and railings are Grade II, NHLE 1265688; the niche in the north-west corner of the forecourt is Grade II*, NHLE 1265687; and the two K6 telephone kiosks outside are Grade II, NHLE 1235680 and NHLE 1235681.
places.history: The buildings are almshouses of 1714, funded by a bequest from Sir Robert Geffrye, a merchant and former Lord Mayor of London. There were fourteen four-room houses for up to 56 pensioners, built for widows of ironmongers, with a large garden behind. The London County Council bought the almshouses and opened them as the Geffrye Museum on 2 April 1914, to serve the local furniture trade with a reference collection of furniture and interiors. The museum closed in January 2018 for an £18 million redevelopment and reopened in June 2021 under the name Museum of the Home, with 80 per cent more exhibition space and 50 per cent more public space.

places.name: St Leonard's Shoreditch
places.summary: St Leonard's Shoreditch stands at the junction of Shoreditch High Street and Hackney Road and works as a parish church. It is Grade I listed, NHLE 1235382, listed on 3 January 1950 as the Church of St Leonard. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The church was designed by George Dance the Elder. Its grid reference on the National Heritage List is TQ 33480 82632, and it is one of the eight Grade I entries inside the Hackney borough boundary.

places.name: Hoxton Hall
places.summary: Hoxton Hall is a working arts venue at 130 Hoxton Street. The building is Grade II* listed, NHLE 1226830, listed on 28 June 1972; Grade II* is the second of the three grades on the National Heritage List. No source states its box-office or building hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The hall was built in 1863 by James Mortimer in the traditional music hall architectural style. James McDonald bought it in 1866 and ran it as McDonald's Music Hall. McDonald expanded the venue in 1867, increasing its capacity, adding a new upper balcony and extending the rear balcony on both sides. The operator states that the hall came through the Second World War undamaged while the nearby Britannia Music Hall was wiped out, and that the basement served as an air raid shelter.

places.name: Shoreditch Town Hall
places.summary: Shoreditch Town Hall is an arts and events venue at 380 Old Street, let as eight distinct hireable spaces. It is Grade II listed, NHLE 1235232, listed on 4 February 1975. No source states general public opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The building's grid reference on the National Heritage List is TQ 33346 82643, inside the Hackney borough boundary despite the EC1V postcode. It was listed on 4 February 1975, the same day as St Mark's Dalston, NHLE 1265134, and the Abney Park mortuary chapel, NHLE 1265023.

places.name: Sutton House
places.address: 2 and 4 Homerton High Street, Hackney, London E9 6JQ
places.summary: Sutton House is a National Trust property at 2 and 4 Homerton High Street. It is Grade II* listed, NHLE 1226810, listed on 24 April 1951, and the gate and piers are separately Grade II, NHLE 1226767. Opening comes as a per-date calendar rather than fixed weekly hours, so no weekly hours are given here. Interiors on show include the Linenfold Parlour, the Great Chamber, the Georgian Parlour, a Tudor kitchen and a recreated squatters' room from the 1980s occupation.
places.history: The house was built in 1535 by Sir Ralph Sadler as his family home and was first known as Bryck Place; Sadler was Principal Secretary of State to Henry VIII. The National Trust bought it in the 1930s with the proceeds of a bequest from William Alexander Robertson, made in memory of his two brothers killed in the First World War. The linenfold panelling was stolen in the 1980s while the building stood derelict and was returned to the National Trust by the salvage firm that recognised its quality. Restoration was completed in 1993 and the house fully opened to the public in 1994.

places.name: St Augustine's Tower
places.address: St John's Church Gardens, Mare Street, Hackney, London E8 1HT
places.summary: St Augustine's Tower stands in St John's Church Gardens off Mare Street and opens to visitors on the last Sunday of every month except December, 2pm to 4.30pm. It is Grade I listed, NHLE 1265635, listed on 24 April 1951 as the Old Tower of Former Church of St Augustine, and it is one of the eight Grade I entries inside the Hackney borough boundary.
places.history: The tower is all that survives above ground of the medieval parish church of St Augustine, which stood on the site until the parish moved to the new church of St John in the 1790s. Its grid reference on the National Heritage List is TQ 34993 85007. The custodians' site dates the structure to 1275 and Wikidata records an inception of 1550; no source states which is right, so no construction date is given here.

places.name: St John-at-Hackney
places.summary: St John-at-Hackney is a parish church on Lower Clapton Road that is also used as a live-music venue. It is Grade II* listed, NHLE 1226959, listed on 24 April 1951 as the Church of St John. No source states general opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The church was designed by James Spiller and replaced the medieval church of St Augustine, whose tower still stands in the churchyard gardens. Five structures in the churchyard carry their own entries on the National Heritage List: the wall to the south-west, Grade II, NHLE 1265589; the war memorial, Grade II, NHLE 1391701; and the Beaufort, Hunter and Loddiges family tombs, Grade II, NHLE 1391333, 1391334 and 1391335. The building's grid reference is TQ 35077 85151.

places.name: Hackney Empire
places.summary: The Hackney Empire is a theatre at 291 Mare Street with a capacity of 1268 for seated shows and 1631 for standing gigs, across Stalls, Dress Circle, Upper Circle and Gallery. The box office opens Monday to Friday, 10am to 6pm, or from two hours before all shows. The building is Grade II* listed, NHLE 1226960, listed on 28 June 1972. Hackney Town Hall next door is Grade II, NHLE 1235869, and its civic garden walls and lamp piers Grade II, NHLE 1235870.
places.history: The theatre opened on 9 December 1901 to a design by Frank Matcham. ATV converted it to television studios in the mid-1950s, broadcasting Take Your Pick and Oh, Boy!. The Mecca Organisation ran it as a bingo hall from 1963 to 1984. Roland Muldoon's campaign secured the freehold in 1986 and returned it to live performance. It closed in 2001 for a £17 million refurbishment by Tim Ronalds Architects and reopened in 2004 with an orchestra pit, a studio theatre and rebuilt stage facilities.

places.name: Broadway Market
places.address: Broadway Market, London Fields, London E8 4QJ
places.summary: Broadway Market runs from London Fields down to the Regent's Canal. The market operator states that it runs 52 weeks a year, 0900 to 1700 on Saturday and 1000 to 1600 on Sunday, and that the street operates 365 days a year. Hackney Council states that the street has been home to market traders since the 1890s and follows an old drovers' route into the City.
places.history: The street itself carries no single designation, and individual buildings on it carry their own entries on the National Heritage List. F Cooke's Eel, Pie and Mash Shop was added to the list on 5 October 2018 at Grade II, NHLE 1458716. Two further pairs of shophouses are Grade II: 75 and 77 Broadway Market, NHLE 1084333, listed on 16 October 1973, and 79 and 81 Broadway Market, NHLE 1084334, listed on 4 February 1975.

places.name: Rio Cinema
places.summary: The Rio Cinema is at 107 Kingsland High Street and is run by a private company limited by guarantee, registered charity number 277415. The building is Grade II listed, NHLE 1244939. Screen 1 seats 402 in total, 188 in the stalls and 214 in the circle, and a 28-seat Screen 2 opened in the basement in December 2017. The operator publishes a telephone line, 020 7241 9410, open 2pm to 8pm daily, rather than building hours.
places.history: A cinema opened on the site in 1909 as the Kingsland Palace; the present building dates from 1915, when the Kingsland Empire opened. F. E. Bromige designed the 1937 Art Deco remodelling of the frontage and auditorium. The building was added to the National Heritage List on 1 February 1999 at Grade II, NHLE 1244939.

places.name: Abney Park Cemetery
places.address: 219 Stoke Newington High Street, London N16 0LH
places.summary: Abney Park Cemetery is at 219 Stoke Newington High Street and opens daily from 8am to dusk, including Christmas Day and New Year's Day. It is a Grade II registered park and garden, NHLE 1000789, with a registered area of 12.59 hectares, about 31 acres. The mortuary chapel is separately Grade II listed, NHLE 1265023, listed on 4 February 1975; the entrance lodges, gates and railings are Grade II, NHLE 1235538; and the walls, gate-piers, railings and gate at the south end are Grade II, NHLE 1365745.
places.history: The cemetery opened in 1840 as a nondenominational garden cemetery with no dividing lines between religious groups, and it belongs to the group of large private London cemeteries known as the Magnificent Seven. The grounds were planted as an arboretum of about 2,500 trees and shrubs, arranged alphabetically and labelled. Roughly 200,000 burials have taken place, with 196,843 recorded up to the year 2000. The chapel was designed by William Hosking, with Joseph Bonomi the Younger and George Collison II, and was complete by 1840. Fourteen monuments inside the cemetery carry their own Grade II entries on the National Heritage List, including those to William and Catherine Booth, NHLE 1257360, Isaac Watts, NHLE 1235434, James Braidwood, NHLE 1257293, and Joanna Vassa, NHLE 1392851.

places.name: Clissold Park and Clissold House
places.address: Clissold House, off Church Street and Green Lanes, London N16 9HJ
places.summary: Clissold Park opens by 7.30am year-round, and closing times vary seasonally from 5pm in January and December to 9.30pm from May to August. It is a Grade II registered park and garden, NHLE 1000800, with a registered area of 22.74 hectares. Clissold House inside it is Grade II* listed, NHLE 1226509, listed on 1 September 1953 under the name Refreshment Rooms. The park is free and the house holds a café and hireable rooms.
places.history: Clissold Park opened as a public park in 1889. The house and park were restored in a project estimated at £8.9 million, begun in 2010 and funded by the Heritage Lottery Fund, the council and the Big Lottery Fund. The council names an aviary and animal enclosures, a paddling area, tennis courts, a wheels park, a pond-dipping platform and an organic growing space among the park's facilities. The New River runs through the park. St Mary's Old Church, Grade II* on the National Heritage List, NHLE 1235419, stands on Stoke Newington Church Street about 24 m outside the registered boundary on its eastern side.

places.name: The Castle Climbing Centre
places.address: The Castle, Green Lanes, London N4 2HA
places.summary: The Castle Climbing Centre occupies the former Metropolitan Water Board engine house on Green Lanes, built in the form of a castle to serve the Stoke Newington reservoirs. It opens Monday to Friday 8am to 10pm, weekends 9am to 8pm and bank holidays 8am to 10pm, and holds a café and a garden. The building is Grade II* listed, NHLE 1226755, listed on 16 May 1972 as the Engine House of Metropolitan Water Board.
places.history: The operator states that the building was once a water pumping station and has spent the last thirty years growing into a climbing centre. Its grid reference on the National Heritage List is TQ 32314 86884. The ancillary building adjoining it to the north carries its own Grade II* entry, NHLE 1235562; the walls and railings to the former pumping station on the west side of Green Lanes are Grade II, NHLE 1390859; and the gas house west of the reservoir is Grade II, NHLE 1265631.

places.name: The Round Chapel
places.summary: The Round Chapel is the former Clapton Park United Reformed Church at 1D Glenarm Road, run as an events and performance venue by Hackney Historic Buildings Trust. It is Grade II* listed, NHLE 1265632, listed on 7 May 1974 under the name United Reformed Church, and is one of the 38 Grade I and Grade II* entries inside the Hackney borough boundary. No source states general opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The building's grid reference on the National Heritage List is TQ 35159 85508, off Lower Clapton Road. The operator describes it as hosting music, film and fashion productions as well as community events, and gives info@hhbt.org.uk as its contact address.

places.name: Hackney Marshes
places.summary: Hackney Marshes is free, unenclosed common land beside the River Lea with 24-hour access, and Hackney Council publishes the address as Homerton Road, London E9 5PF. The council counts 82 football, rugby and cricket pitches across North Marsh, South Marsh and Mabley Green.
places.history: The council describes the marshes as internationally known as the spiritual home of Sunday league football, and the site holds a Green Flag award. Homerton station is about 1.2 km away.

places.name: Springfield Park
places.summary: Springfield Park is open 24 hours a day, and Springfield House and its café open 10am to 6pm from April to September and 10am to 4pm from October to March. The park is a Grade II registered park and garden, NHLE 1000839, with a registered area of 13.44 hectares; Hackney Council gives the managed park as 14.73 hectares, the difference being the boundary on the National Heritage List against the park the council runs.
places.history: Springfield Park officially opened as a public park in 1905, formed from the grounds of three private houses, of which Springfield House survives. Its grid reference on the National Heritage List is TQ 34629 87518. The park slopes down to the River Lea and the Springfield Marina.

links.note: The Regent's Canal runs from Hackney into Tower Hamlets, and Victoria Park, NHLE 1000178, adjoins Hackney but is a Tower Hamlets park.
The Regent's Canal runs west into Islington; Newington Green straddles the boundary, and 52-55 Newington Green, Grade I, NHLE 1293320, is Islington's.
The Regent's Canal continues west from Hackney to Hampstead Road Lock in Camden, the canal structure Camden carries as a place of its own.

entries.name: Museum of the Home
entries.note: Free entry with no booking, 10am to 5pm Tuesday to Sunday, in the Geffrye almshouses of 1714 at 136 Kingsland Road, Grade I, NHLE 1226772.

entries.name: Sutton House
entries.note: A National Trust house built in 1535 for Sir Ralph Sadler, showing the Linenfold Parlour, the Great Chamber and a recreated squatters' room from the 1980s.

entries.name: St Augustine's Tower
entries.note: Open the last Sunday of every month except December, 2pm to 4.30pm; all that survives above ground of the medieval parish church, Grade I, NHLE 1265635.

entries.name: Hackney Empire
entries.note: Frank Matcham's theatre of 9 December 1901, 1268 seated or 1631 standing; the box office opens Monday to Friday 10am to 6pm or two hours before shows.

entries.name: Broadway Market
entries.note: 0900 to 1700 on Saturday and 1000 to 1600 on Sunday, 52 weeks a year, on a street trading since the 1890s; F Cooke's is Grade II, NHLE 1458716.

entries.note: A 1915 cinema with F. E. Bromige's 1937 Art Deco frontage, 402 seats in Screen 1 and 28 in the basement Screen 2 opened in December 2017.

entries.name: Clissold Park and Clissold House
entries.note: 22.74 hectares with the New River running through, open from 7.30am; Clissold House holds a café and is Grade II*, NHLE 1226509.

entries.note: A former Metropolitan Water Board engine house built as a castle, open Monday to Friday 8am to 10pm and weekends 9am to 8pm, with a café and garden.

entries.name: St Leonard's Shoreditch
entries.note: George Dance the Elder's parish church at the junction of Shoreditch High Street and Hackney Road, Grade I, NHLE 1235382.

entries.name: Hoxton Hall
entries.note: A music hall of 1863 by James Mortimer, enlarged in 1867 with a new upper balcony, still working as an arts venue at 130 Hoxton Street.

entries.name: Shoreditch Town Hall
entries.note: An arts and events venue at 380 Old Street let as eight distinct hireable spaces; check its programme, since no source states general opening hours.

entries.name: St John-at-Hackney
entries.note: James Spiller's church of the 1790s, Grade II*, NHLE 1226959, working as a parish church and a live-music venue on Lower Clapton Road.

entries.name: The Round Chapel
entries.note: The former Clapton Park United Reformed Church, Grade II*, NHLE 1265632, run by Hackney Historic Buildings Trust for music, film and community events.

entries.name: Hackney Marshes
entries.note: Unenclosed common land beside the River Lea with 24-hour access and 82 football, rugby and cricket pitches across North Marsh, South Marsh and Mabley Green.

entries.name: Springfield Park
entries.note: Open at all hours, sloping to the River Lea and the Springfield Marina; the house and café open 10am to 6pm April to September, 10am to 4pm October to March.
